items.title: Lead isotopes trace Malawi's mysterious copper ingot hoard to Congo's Kipushi mine
items.summary: In 1967, a Malawian farmer stumbled upon a hidden hoard of eight copper ingots buried beneath a tree. Now, more than half a century later, scientists have traced the metal to its source: a copper mine nearly 800 km (500 miles) away.

items.title: Molecular 'self-destruct' switch discovered: How stressed cells decide between survival and death
items.summary: A new study from Ben-Gurion University of the Negev (BGU) has identified a molecular switch that controls whether stressed human cells activate a survival mechanism or trigger programmed cell death (apoptosis). items.title: Digital textbooks significantly boost students' intrinsic learning motivation
items.summary: A research team from The Education University of Hong Kong (EdUHK) and East China Normal University (ECNU) has published a meta-analysis demonstrating the impact of digital textbooks (DTs) on student motivation. items.title: Millions in the US Northeast brace for a powerful storm
items.summary: More than 40 million people in the northeastern United States braced Friday for heavy rain and strong winds as an unusually powerful storm for the season was forecast to crash into the region.

items.title: Canals full, roads submerged as Bangkok declares flood disaster
items.summary: Bangkok authorities declared a flood disaster across the Thai capital on Saturday after almost 48 hours of heavy rain left canals full, roads submerged and residents wading through deep water.

items.title: Indonesia fires threaten critically endangered orangutan: IUCN
items.summary: Wildfires that tore through Indonesian Borneo's vast tropical forests have increased pressure on critically endangered Bornean orangutans, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) said Saturday.

items.title: Guatemala ensures survival of vulnerable 'fossil' fish
items.summary: In a freshwater canal surrounded by mangroves in southern Guatemala, hundreds of baby tropical gars—a torpedo-shaped fish with an alligator-like snout dubbed the "fossil fish"—are released into the wild.

items.summary: An estimated 38 trillion bacteria live in the human body—and only a small fraction are harmful to our health. However, the harmful ones can cause serious illness, especially when they develop resistance to antibiotics.

items.title: Climate crisis is affecting children's nutrition
items.summary: Wildfires, floods and other extreme weather events are no longer the only ways climate change affects children around the world. Increasingly, it also affects their diets. items.summary: During a news conference at 3 p.m. EDT on Monday, Sept. 28, NASA and Boeing leadership will discuss Starliner’s development and plans for regular crew flights to and from the International Space Station. items.title: Breaking and entering: How parasites prepare host cells for invasion
items.summary: Before the parasite Toxoplasma gondii can invade a cell, it has to know it has reached the right place. New research from the Whitehead Institute reveals that the parasite doesn't simply recognize a ready-made doorway into the cell. Instead, it helps create the conditions for its own entry.

items.title: How cells rapidly detect viruses that fuse with their membranes
items.summary: Researchers have figured out a missing piece of the puzzle of how human cells detect invading viruses and mount an immune response within an hour.

items.summary: Slaughterhouses are places most people never want to go, and might seem like unlikely places to search for rare or endangered species. items.title: Mitochondrial protein complexes: A single amino acid can jeopardize their stability
items.summary: Removing a single amino acid can determine whether new proteins assemble into stable complexes within mitochondria. items.title: Blood pressure enzyme reveals second job: Making sulfur rings for cellular antioxidants
items.summary: Antioxidants such as vitamins C and E protect cells by neutralizing free radicals, such as reactive oxygen species, before they can damage genetic material or cell membranes. items.title: Natural proteins can guide active ingredients to diseased cells
items.summary: After taking a pill, the drugs it contains are distributed throughout the body, reaching the tissues and cells affected by disease and performing their intended function. However, they also enter healthy cells, where they often cause more harm than good.

items.title: How a century-old solvent can enable efficient amide synthesis
items.summary: Amide bonds are chemical linkages essential to biology, medicine and materials chemistry. Peptide bonds, a class of amide bonds, link amino acids to form proteins. Amide bonds are also important in medicines and polymers. Efficient synthesis of amide bonds remains a major focus in green chemistry.

items.title: Ultrathin materials could make quantum light circuits programmable
items.summary: Quantum photonics could be a pivotal part of future quantum technology if the right materials can be created, a new review paper has found.

items.summary: Spacecraft propulsion traditionally relies on volatile fuels and separate, bulky systems for different types of maneuvering in space. NASA is working to change that paradigm. items.title: Laser light enables detection of colorectal cancer biomarker in blood within minutes
items.summary: Researchers often use antibodies to detect specific molecules or biological markers because they are remarkably precise at recognizing their targets. However, finding the faint signals of cancer in blood samples is a challenge even for the most reliable techniques.

items.title: New tools pinpoint where urban trees could provide the most relief from heat
items.summary: Cities trying to cool sweltering streets often set broad tree canopy targets. But those targets can overlook the reality that not all shade is equally useful, and not every neighborhood has room for more trees.

items.title: Previously overlooked protein helps cells divide correctly
items.summary: Modern technologies have made it possible to uncover a growing "hidden proteome"—proteins encoded by parts of the genome that researchers previously overlooked. items.summary: What are the chances of finding extraterrestrial life in our solar system? items.title: Plant root injuries unleash pressure waves that travel long distances
items.summary: When plant roots are injured—by insects, for example—the pressure inside the root drops, and a pressure wave spreads rapidly throughout the root system. In neighboring roots, tiny proteins that act as mechanical pressure sensors detect the change and generate electrical and calcium signals.

items.title: Pompeii's destruction helps calibrate volcanic dating to within decades
items.summary: When Pliny the Younger recorded his firsthand experience of the eruption of Mount Vesuvius 2,000 years ago—a cataclysm that buried Pompeii and killed his uncle, Pliny the Elder—he provided enough detail about the date to allow scientists to benchmark methods for dating volcanic eruptions.

items.title: Scientists supercharge plant immunity to boost its natural defense response
items.summary: Nanyang Technological University, Singapore (NTU Singapore) scientists have developed a way to "supercharge" a plant's natural immune response.

items.title: Freezing threatens mRNA delivery, but Tris buffer helps nanoparticles retain their potency
items.summary: Researchers at The University of Texas at Austin have teamed up with pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly and Company to uncover how storage conditions affect mRNA lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), the technology behind COVID-19 vaccines and other treatments, and how to make them more effective.

items.summary: SKA-Low is a radio telescope under construction in Western Australia. items.summary: We are continuously sending information to each other, transmitting zeros and ones through a giant network of connected computers and devices. items.title: Q&A: Were small down payments to blame for the housing bubble?
items.summary: The U.S. housing bubble of the early 2000s sent home prices soaring before the market crashed in 2007–08, triggering a foreclosure crisis and a deep recession.

items.title: Discovery confirms rare, switchable electrical property in widely used electronics material
items.summary: A Husker research team's latest research could open the door to broader use of a class of materials whose electrical properties may someday power next-generation electronics, high-density energy storage, improved computer memory and new strategies for cooling.

items.title: Webb detects ammonia and unexpected chill on a distant giant planet
items.summary: Using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), a team of astronomers led by the University of Maryland identified water, methane and ammonia in the atmosphere of HATS-6 b, a giant planet 500 light-years from Earth. items.title: Students help researchers study how people experience temperature
items.summary: Are there any geographical differences in how people experience weather conditions? This question was investigated in the citizen science project Kallt och svettigt (Cold and sweaty) for a year with the help of school pupils throughout Sweden.

items.title: Private spacecraft falls back to Earth after failing to rescue aging NASA telescope
items.summary: The robotic spacecraft that failed to rescue an aging NASA telescope plunged back to Earth on Friday less than three months after launching on the bold mission.

items.title: Personal experience trumps public reputation when people judge others' refusals
items.summary: A research team led by Professor Hitoshi Yamamoto of Rissho University experimentally examined how people evaluate others when a person's public reputation conflicts with their own experience with that person. The study was published Sept. 14, 2026, in the journal Evolution and Human Behavior.

items.title: Molecular switch-up: Bacteria remodel a peptide to take on new role
items.summary: Remodeling may bring to mind construction crews and scaffolding, but the process is far from unique to buildings. Even molecules can be remodeled. Pandorachelins, newly discovered molecules produced by Pandoraea bacteria, are one example.

items.title: The Uprising: The real medieval revolt that inspired Andrew Garfield's new film
items.summary: The Uprising, a medieval drama directed by Paul Greengrass and starring Andrew Garfield, is set to hit theaters this fall. The film draws its inspiration from the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 in England.

items.title: Targeted nanoparticles reduce tumor scarring and enable immunotherapy response in mice
items.summary: Many liver and lung cancers arise in tissue that's already been scarred by chronic disease, such as hepatitis, cirrhosis or long-term lung damage. items.title: Researchers track emerging pathogens at Arctic bird gathering
items.summary: Every year, birds migrate north and gather in a single location in the Arctic, and a team of University of Kentucky researchers is collaborating with Alaska Native communities to study how diseases spread and evolve at this gathering before they reach human populations.

items.title: African elephants and medicinal plants: Possible self-medication documented through local ecological knowledge
items.summary: Wild African elephants living in the Mount Elgon region of Kenya appear to seek out specific plants when unwell. Local experts also reported mothers administering plant-based "medicine" to their offspring.

items.title: Trade tensions, high prices and interest rates drive slip in consumers' outlook
items.summary: Consumer sentiment fell by less than four index points in September, reaching its lowest reading in four months and down 15% from January 2026, according to the University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers.

items.title: Two ancient burial sites may explain mystery of Göbeklitepe's scattered human bones
items.summary: Since 1995, archaeologists have excavated hundreds of human bones from Göbeklitepe, an archaeological site in southeastern Türkiye. The ancient remains are around 10,000 years old and date to a time when humans were beginning to settle into permanent farming communities.

items.title: Gen Z communicates differently in the workplace, but older colleagues can still decode them
items.summary: For all the talk about generational differences at work, some of the biggest differences show up in surprisingly ordinary moments.

items.title: Teen loneliness may follow young people into the workplace
items.summary: What happens when loneliness follows a young person from the school hallway into the workplace? New research suggests that feeling lonely during adolescence may be linked to a greater risk of unstable or less secure employment in young adulthood.

items.title: Climate overshoot will leave lasting impacts even after global temperatures fall
items.summary: Returning global temperatures to a climate target does not necessarily undo the damage caused by exceeding it, new Concordia-led research published in the journal Communications Earth & Environment finds.

items.title: Age, not feed additives, affects antimicrobial resistance genes in chickens
items.summary: For many years, antibiotics have been added to animal feed to help control harmful bacteria and improve growth.
